newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Burma, Laos join ASEAN but Cambodia still looms.
newsitem.headline: Burma, Laos join ASEAN but Cambodia still looms.

text.p: ASEAN formally admitted new members Burma and Laos on Wednesday, but left unsettled the sticky question of Cambodia's membership in the regional grouping even as Phnom Penh welcomed mediation in the crisis.

Foreign ministers of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) met for three hours earlier on Wednesday to discuss Cambodia and a bid by Foreign Minister Ung Huot to assuage ASEAN concerns over the turmoil in his country.
But Cambodia's last-minute plea to be formally inducted in the now nine-member group on Wednesday went unfulfilled.
In a surprise about-face, Cambodia even said on Wednesday that it would welcome ASEAN mediation, when a week ago Second Prime Minister Hun Sen told foreigners to stay out of Cambodia's business.
"If we don't join (ASEAN), it won't be the death of us," Hun Sen said last week.
ASEAN stuck by its July 10 decision to postpone indefinitely Cambodia's membership following Hun Sen's bloody ouster of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
Asian diplomats in Phnom Penh welcomed the Cambodian government's apparent about-face on mediation, but said they were waiting to hear the premier announce the policy himself.
"It's a statement to make peace again with ASEAN but it would be more credible if Hun Sen acknowledged it himself," one diplomat said. "It's a step forward for whatever it's worth," he said.

Another diplomat said Ung Huot was possibly trying to sway ASEAN ministers over letting Cambodia in on Wednesday. "It was a move to get ASEAN to reconsider. Hun Sen probably told him to say whatever he had to say," the diplomat said.

The persuasion apparently didn't work. Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told a brief news conference on Wednesday: "We feel there is still instability in Cambodia, and we reaffirmed our decision (of July 10) not to induct Cambodia on the 23rd."
ASEAN, celebrating its 30th year, now comprises Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei, Burma and Laos.

A senior ASEAN source said it was highly unlikely Cambodia would be admitted in the near future. He said it was more likely to happen during an annual ASEAN summit in December if the situation in Cambodia is straightened out, "although in politics anything can happen".

Abdullah said the foreign ministers of Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines would meet Ung Huot and then report back to a full ministerial meeting. The ministers are due to meet with the Cambodian foreign minister on Wednesday evening to discuss the mediation process.
An ASEAN source said there was still some question over Ung Huot's status as head of Cambodia's observer delegation at the group's annual two-day foreign ministerial meeting opening on Thursday.
"That is something still to be clarified also," the source said.
Abdullah said ASEAN still regarded Ranariddh as first prime minister despite his ousting by Hun Sen.
Ung Huot has been named to replace Ranariddh, who on Tuesday urged ASEAN not to accept the foreign minister as Cambodia's representative.

The lengthy midday session and Abdullah's subsequent news conference delayed the formal induction of Burma and Laos by at least 30 minutes. ASEAN brushed aside Western criticism of Burma's record on human rights and democracy to bring it into the fold.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas discussed Cambodia on Wednesday with U.S. President Bill Clinton's special envoy, former congressman Stephen Solarz.

"We very much want to work with our friends in ASEAN and other countries in the region," Solarz, who is on an Asian trip to help find a solution to the Cambodian issue, told reporters after the meeting.
Alatas also told reporters he and Solarz had agreed "that we should continue to keep in touch with one another and to cooperate with one another".
Alatas showed a flash of anger when asked why Burma should be allowed to join ASEAN and Cambodia kept out.

"Clearly, objectively, something has happened in Cambodia...has resulted in fighting, in instability, in turmoil in Cambodia, and we in ASEAN asked ourselves whether in that condition Cambodia...could assume its rights and responsibilities as a full-fledged member," he said.
No such conditions prevailed in Burma, he said.
Four demonstrators gathered outside a fast-food shop near the conference hotel on Wednesday to protest on behalf of the Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma against Rangoon's accession.
Under strict Malaysian laws, five or more people need a permit to demonstrate.
The Network said in a statement Burma's admittance was "a mark of shame to people of the region who value human rights, justice, democracy and peace".
